title: Adverse reaction to metal debris with accompanying gout and amyloid deposits in hip arthroplasty
case_text: A 71-year-old man presented with a 13-year history of a left metal-on-metal total hip arthroplasty and several weeks of progressive left hip and groin pain. He denied fever, chills, trauma, neurologic symptoms, or prior gout or amyloidosis. His medical history was notable for MPO/p-ANCA–positive vasculitis treated with low-dose rituximab. On examination, there was no erythema or drainage at the surgical scar, and he walked without assistance. Laboratory studies showed a C-reactive protein level above normal and a normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate; serum cobalt was elevated and chromium was not. Pelvic radiographs revealed well-seated bilateral hip prostheses without periprosthetic lucency or visible debris. MRI with metal-artifact reduction demonstrated distention of the left hip joint capsule with complex fluid and surrounding soft-tissue edema, and a focus of metallic debris along the iliac bone. Fluoroscopically guided aspiration of the left hip yielded 16 mL of cloudy brown fluid. Analysis showed a red-cell count of 234,000 /µL, a white-cell count of 11,650 /µL, negative aerobic and anaerobic cultures, and fluid positive for cobalt, chromium, and monosodium urate crystals.
article_excerpt:
Background Historically, metal-on-metal (MoM) implants were considered a biomechanically favorable option for patients requiring total hip arthroplasty implants: they have less volumetric wear and low failure rates due to wear-induced osteolysis, and have the ability to contain larger femoral heads that increase stability

. However, over time MoM implants started to show increasing revision rates attributed to the release of metal particles in the periprosthetic space creating a spectrum of findings that are termed adverse reaction to metal debris (ARMD)

. Diagnosis of ARMD related prosthesis failure is typically indicated by an abnormally elevated serum cobalt level, but concomitant diagnoses may also be identified and may complicate the interpretation of abnormal lab results. One previous case report identified 2 patients with concurrent ARMD and crystalline arthropathy (one patient with monosodium urate and the other with calcium pyrophosphate crystals aspirated), emphasizing the complexity of symptomatic ARMD while concluding that the crystalline arthropathy was not the primary cause of symptomatic hip inflammation

. Furthermore, we were unable to find a case of ARMD with concurrent amyloid deposition in the literature. We present a unique case of ARMD with accompanying monosodium urate crystals and amyloid deposition in the hip of a patient who had undergone a MoM hip arthroplasty. This is the only published case to date of a patient with these 3 co-existing conditions. Case presentation A 71-year-old male presented with left hip/groin pain. He had a history of a MoM left hip arthroplasty performed 13 years prior to presentation. The components were a Zimmer CLS #8 cementless femoral stem, 135-degree femoral neck, 50 mm head, plus 4 mm neck, and 56 mm Duracon acetabulum. He also had a right total hip arthroplasty that was placed 21 years prior. The arthroplasties were performed for osteoarthritis. He denied any recent trauma. He reported no fevers or chills. No neurologic symptoms were described. He had a history of MPO/p-ANCA positive vasculitis for which he was on low dose rituximab. He had no other relevant medical or surgical history. In particular, there was no history of gout or amyloidosis. His BMI was 27 kg/m 2 . There was no erythema or drainage from the surgical scar. He was able to walk without any assistive devices. Blood tests revealed elevated CRP and normal ESR. Further blood tests revealed elevated cobalt and negative chromium. Radiographs demonstrated bilateral total hip arthroplasties with well-seated components ( Fig. 1 ). No periprosthetic lucency or metallic debris was visible. Subsequent MRI with metal artifact reduction revealed distention of the left hip joint capsule with surrounding edema extending into the adjacent muscles and around the femoral vessels and sciatic nerve ( Fig. 2 ). Prominent metallic debris was seen superiorly along the left iliac bone, presumed to have migrated there via the iliopsoas bursa ( Fig. 3 ). Fluoroscopically-guided aspiration of the left hip with an 18-gauge needle yielded 16 mL of cloudy brown fluid ( Figs. 4 and 5 ). The aspirated fluid was positive for cobalt and chromium, and was also positive for monosodium urate crystals. The synovial RBC count was 234,000 /μL and the WBC count was 11,650 /μL with differential unable to be performed due to degenerated cells. Aerobic and anaerobic cultures were negative for organisms. Findings were compatible with ARMD in the setting of a MoM hip arthroplasty. Fig. 1 (a) Low-centered AP radiograph of the pelvis and (b) lateral radiograph of the left hip demonstrate a metal-on-metal left total hip arthroplasty. There is also a right total hip arthroplasty with a metal-on-polyethylene design. Suture anchors are present in the bilateral greater trochanters. No metallic debris is visible radiographically. Fig 1 Fig. 2 (a) Axial T1 and (b) axial STIR images from MRI of the left hip using a MAVRIC protocol for metal artifact reduction. These demonstrate distention of the hip joint capsule due to complex fluid/synovitis, best seen along the femoral neck anteriorly (white arrows). There is surrounding edema. (c) Axial STIR image shows a metallic particle posterior to the left hip (red arrow). (d) Axial STIR image shows edema-like signal around the left proximal femur extending to the femoral vessels (blue arrow) and sciatic nerve (orange arrow). Non-enlarged hyperintense left inguinal lymph nodes are noted (green arrow). Fig 2 Fig. 3 (a) Coronal T1 and (b) coronal STIR images from MRI of the left hip. These demonstrate a low signal intensity structure along the medial aspect of the left iliac bone, compatible with metallic debris (red arrows). The left hip arthroplasty is seen with distention of the joint capsule, particularly along the medial aspect of the femoral neck (white arrows). Fig 3 Fig. 4 Intraprocedural image during fluoroscopically guided aspiration of the left hip showing the needle tip projecting at the neck of the femoral prosthesis. Fig 4 Fig. 5 Aspiration of the left hip yielded 16 mL of cloudy brown fluid. Fig 5 The patient underwent revision of the left total hip arthroplasty, including the entire acetabular component and the femoral head with placement of a polyethylene liner ( Fig. 6 ). Thick pseudocapsule formation, milky joint fluid, and sub-centimeter areas of osteolysis were noted at the time of surgery. Pathologic examination of the left hip joint capsule revealed focal deposits of amyloid by Congo red stain ( Fig. 7 ). The post-operative course was complicated by capsular dehiscence and subcutaneous fluid collection. Fig. 6 Post-operative low-centered AP radiograph of the pelvis demonstrates interval revision of the left total hip arthroplasty, now with a metal-on-polyethylene design. The right hip arthroplasty is unchanged. Fig 6 Fig. 7 Congo red stained left hip joint capsule section examined under polarized light shows apple-green birefringence, indicating amyloid positivity. The amount of amyloid was small and not enough for sub-typing. Original magnification 200×. Fig 7 Discussion ARMD is a known complication of MoM articulations, which generate metal ions and particulate debris from corrosive wear leading to the stimulation of immune responses. ARMD is also referred to as “adverse local tissue reaction” which is a term used to describe a plethora of histological findings associated with immune system activation

,

,

. The most common symptoms and physical exam findings in ARMD are hip/groin pain. Systemic symptoms such as vision loss, hearing loss, and cardiac problems are rare but can occur with long term metal toxicity. Blood tests commonly show elevated CRP and cobalt levels [ 6 , 7 ]. Synovial fluid analysis may serve as a useful screening tool for ARMD and other pathologies, and is important in ruling out infection

. Radiographs and MRI (optimized for metal artifact reduction) are the main imaging modalities used in the work-up of ARMD. Common MRI findings include increased joint fluid, synovial thickening, low signal intensity debris, soft tissue edema, and abductor disruption. Ultrasound and CT may also be used but have a relatively lower sensitivity/specificity when it comes to ARMD identification

. Crystal deposits are commonly seen in cases of crystalline arthropathy such as gout and pseudogout. These 2 conditions may present suddenly with accompanying swelling, pain, and stiffness around the affected joint

. The pathogenesis involves monosodium urate (gout) or calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout) crystal deposits within a joint leading to the initiation of an acute inflammatory cascade

. Risk factors for crystalline arthropathy include age, diet, weight, family history, and recent surgical procedures. A common diagnostic procedure includes synovial fluid aspiration in which the presence of crystals can confirm crystalline arthropathy. Treatments are designed to focus on the reduction of inflammation while also working to lower the amount of uric acid in the blood

. There have been 2 documented cases where crystalline arthropathy has been seen in conjunction with ARMD, both of which were confirmed with synovial fluid aspiration. It is unclear if crystalline arthropathy may be a result or cause of ARMD. However, a possible etiology of the accompanying crystalline arthropathy includes the change in joint space pH (acidosis) due to ARMD, which can trigger the development/insoluble state of urate crystals leading to gout

. Crystalline arthropathy has been reported to resolve following MoM hip arthroplasty revision, further suggesting an association. While it is important to note that crystalline arthropathy is not reported as the cause of hip arthroplasty failures, it may play a role in the associated symptoms. We report a case of ARMD with accompanying monosodium urate crystals as well as amyloid deposition in the hip of a patient who had undergone MoM hip arthroplasty. Amyloid arthropathy is a disease that is characterized by the deposition of insoluble protein fibrils in the tissue, most notably transthyretin and apolipoprotein A-I. However, some patients, similar to our patient, have unclassified amyloid owing to paucity of amyloid deposits

. Amyloid deposition around joint tissues and synovia can cause the affected joint to develop pain and edema which can be misdiagnosed as gout or rheumatoid arthritis

. Amyloid deposits are best identified on pathologic examination via Congo red stain examined under polarized light. Amyloid deposits consist of aggregates of certain proteins which are susceptible to misfolding with changes in pH. We hypothesize that the accompanying urate crystal deposits as well as the amyloid deposits occur due to a change in joint space pH. The acidic environment that develops from ARMD may predispose to urate crystal deposits; if the pH drops low enough it may also cause protein misfolding and amyloid formation within the joint space. In other words, both crystalline arthropathy and amyloid arthropathy may be downstream effects of ARMD in patients with MoM hip arthroplasties and should not be treated in isolation. It is advised to screen for both urate crystals and amyloid plaques when creating a treatment plan for ARMD. Conclusion We presented a patient with a history of MoM hip arthroplasty who complained of acute hip pain. This patient was diagnosed with ARMD along with co-existing urate crystal formation found prior to revision surgery and amyloid deposits found post-operatively, a combination which has not been previously described. We report this case to alert the orthopedist that crystalline arthropathy and amyloid deposits may present at the same time as ARMD, potentially a result of alterations in pH due to ARMD. Serum and synovial laboratory tests along with pathological examination may be abnormal because of crystal or amyloid development. The orthopedist should be aware of these possible co-existing conditions; ARMD often predominates the clinical picture but these other processes could accentuate symptomatology and potentially complicate the post-operative course. Patient consent Written informed consent for the publication of this case report was obtained from the patient.

title: Pseudotumor in total knee revision arthroplasty resembling heterotopic ossification: A case report
case_text: A 65-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis, hypercholesterolemia, asthma, and hypertension presented with a three-year history of a progressively enlarging, asymptomatic mass in the posterior aspect of the left knee. He had undergone a primary left total knee arthroplasty 40 years earlier and a two-stage revision 30 years ago for prosthetic joint infection. On examination, the popliteal mass was firm, fixed, and non-tender. Knee range of motion was 0° to 90°, patellar tracking and ligamentous stability were intact, and functional knee tests were negative. He denied fever, chills, or constitutional symptoms. Laboratory studies were unremarkable: WBC 6.8 × 10^9/L, ESR 28 mm/h, and CRP 3.0 mg/L. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs showed lucency around the tibial component and a periarticular reaction with multiple irregular, well-circumscribed hyperdense regions highly suggestive of heterotopic ossification. Doppler ultrasound revealed a non-cystic 11.6 × 4.0 × 7.2 cm mass without detectable blood flow. Given the mass’s size, persistent growth, and indeterminate imaging features, a biopsy was planned to exclude malignancy.
article_excerpt:
1 Introduction Total joint arthroplasty (TJA) is one of the most common elective orthopedic procedures worldwide and is projected to reach nearly one million cases annually by 2040.  Due to the widespread use of orthopedic implants, there is continuous discussion regarding their associated complications and ways to improve outcomes. A significant concern in TJA is the development of immunologic and inflammatory responses triggered by prosthetic devices . Metallosis, a metal-induced synovitis, arises from friction between the implants' interfaces, which releases debris and induces a foreign-body inflammatory reaction . Pseudotumors are well-recognized soft tissue masses occurring secondary to metallosis. They are characterized as non-neoplastic, non-infectious, solid, or cystic processes that arise in the proximity of implants and frequently extend beyond the articular joint capsule . The pathophysiology behind pseudotumor formation has not been fully elucidated, but two main mechanisms have been proposed: hypersensitivity to metal ions and local high-wear debris . The occurrence of pseudotumors following total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is uncommon, but the true incidence remains poorly described. In contrast, the emergence of pseudotumors in the setting of total hip arthroplasty (THA) is significant, reported in up to 69 % of patients . This difference is mainly attributed to the prevalent utilization of polyethylene (PE) as the bearing surface in TKA procedures, avoiding direct metal-on-metal (MoM) contact . Given the limited data of pseudotumors following TKA and the relatively nonspecific presentation, physicians may not routinely consider them as part of the differential diagnosis of periprosthetic masses. While many patients are asymptomatic, pseudotumors are not devoid of complications. They pose an increased risk of implant loosening and revision surgery, highlighting the potential socioeconomic burden placed on affected patients . Despite growing interest in the topic, the available evidence of pseudotumors after TKA remains scarce. In this report, we present the case of a retired 65-year-old male with an atypical presentation of a pseudotumor resembling heterotopic ossification (HO) after revision TKA. The case is presented in line with the updated consensus-based surgical case report (SCARE) guidelines . 2 Presentation of case A 65-year-old male with a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis, hypercholesterolemia, asthma, and hypertension presented to the clinic after noticing a palpable mass on the posterior aspect of the left knee. Approximately forty years ago, he underwent a left TKA due to degenerative joint disease. Ten years later, a two-stage revision was performed due to a prosthetic joint infection (PJI), reimplanting a hinge knee prosthesis twelve weeks afterward. The patient first noticed the mass three years ago but remained able to ambulate without difficulty or pain. However, he observed a consistent enlargement over time, which prompted him to seek medical evaluation. Following a physical examination and review of imaging studies, the reconstructive surgery specialist considered HO to be the underlying diagnosis. Nonetheless, due to the mass's pronounced size and persistent growth, the surgeon referred the patient to a musculoskeletal oncology specialist for further assessment. Upon evaluation at our clinic, the patient remained asymptomatic and denied any limitations in his daily activities. No constitutional symptoms (i.e., fever, chills, malaise, fatigue) were reported. The physical exam revealed a rigid, fixed, non-tender mass in the left popliteal fossa. The patient demonstrated adequate patellar tracking, ligamentous balancing, and an adequate range of motion (0° to 90°). Relevant functional knee tests were performed, all yielding negative results. Infectious workup was within normal ranges, including white blood cell count [(WBC), 6.8 × 10 9 /L], erythrocyte sedimentation rate [(ESR), 28 mm/h], and C-reactive protein [(CRP), 3.0 mg/L]. Anteroposterior (AP) and lateral radiographs of the left knee revealed an area of lucency surrounding the tibial component concerning for loosening. There was a significant periarticular reaction with multiple regions of well-circumscribed but irregular hyperdense patterns, highly suggestive of extensive HO ( Fig. 1 ). Moreover, Doppler ultrasound findings showed a non-cystic mass of approximately 11.6 cm × 4.0 cm × 7.2 cm without detectable blood flow ( Fig. 2 ). Based on these radiologic findings, coupled with the concerning features (i.e., pronounced size and persistent growth), a malignant etiology could not be excluded; therefore, we considered a mass biopsy. The patient was fully informed about his clinical scenario and treatment alternatives. After discussing the procedures' risks and benefits, he underwent an open biopsy of the mass without procedural complications. Fig. 1 Radiographs demonstrating a periarticular reaction on the left knee with multiple areas of irregular hyperdense patterns concerning for heterotopic ossification. Fig. 1 Fig. 2 Doppler Ultrasound showing the mass on the left posterior knee. Fig. 2 At the first postoperative visit, the patient was doing well, the surgical incision was healing properly, and the knee's range of motion was preserved. The pathology report revealed several irregular grayish-black fibroconnective tissue fragments consistent with a pseudotumor ( Fig. 3 ). After excluding a malignant etiology and educating the patient regarding his diagnosis, we recommended re-evaluation by his joint replacement specialist for further management. At his most recent follow-up (i.e., one year), the patient remains without symptoms and high functionality; he is not interested in further management. Fig. 3 Pathology slides showing the knee pseudotumor in hematoxylin and eosin stain in low-power (A) and high-power microscopy (B). Fig. 3 3 Discussion We have reported the atypical case of a 65-year-old male patient who developed a pseudotumor following a revision TKA. The patient exhibited a progressively growing mass in the left posterior knee without associated symptoms. Radiographs revealed multiple irregular, hyperdense areas surrounding the joint. The initial assessment suggested HO as the underlying etiology based on these findings. However, the definitive diagnosis of a pseudotumor was established only after histopathological examination of the mass. The pathophysiology of pseudotumor formation is poorly understood but has been attributed to the released debris from the friction between metallic prostheses [

,

,

, 9 ]. This debris is deposited in the soft tissue, triggering the recruitment of inflammatory cells that infiltrate the synovium, inducing its hyperplasia to enclose the debris . These tumor-like masses have been frequently described following THA, accredited to metal-on-metal prostheses [ 5 , 10 ]. However, recent studies have found an increasing association of pseudotumors with non-metal-on-metal components, extending their recognition in TKA . Using PE as the bearing surface in these procedures eliminates direct metal-on-metal contact. Therefore, their emergence in this setting is likely due to abnormal metallic interaction following advanced PE wear or detachment . These mechanisms allow friction at the tibiofemoral or patellofemoral components . High cross-linked PE and all-PE patellar prosthetic prostheses have largely replaced prior designs, addressing this concern [ 13 , 14 ]. However, there is still a considerable prevalence of patients with outdated implants at an increased risk of abnormal metal-on-metal interaction in TKA. The presentation of pseudotumors is relatively non-specific [ 2 , 15 , 16 ]. However, some may present with complications such as functional impairment, leg swelling, and claudication [

,

,

]. Additionally, pseudotumors pose an increased risk for implant loosening, which allows for increased motion and abrasion between the bearing surfaces, generating further debris and inflammation . The differential diagnosis of a periprosthetic mass following TKA includes soft tissue or bone sarcomas, metastatic carcinomas, aneurysms of the popliteal artery, and heterotopic ossification, among others [

,

,

]. Given their rare occurrence, vague presentation, and limited available data, physicians may overlook pseudotumors during diagnostic assessment. Radiographs are the initial step in evaluating pseudotumors; however, definitive diagnostic criteria have not been established. As a result, findings are generally indeterminate and have poor sensitivity [ 21 , 22 ]. Sonographic features of pseudotumors may vary from a cystic fluid collection with heterogeneous echogenicity to a solid mass without significant fluid components. Moreover, these masses lack significant vascularity on Doppler ultrasound . Additional imaging studies, such as Computed Tomography (CT) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), may further characterize and differentiate between pseudotumors and other periprosthetic masses . In contrast to the rare incidence of pseudotumors in TKA, HO has been reported in up to 40 % of cases [ 23 , 24 ]. HO is characterized by the abnormal formation of bone in soft tissue and muscles, typically appearing periarticular.  Radiographically, findings shift and evolve as bone maturation progresses . Initially, no ossification can be seen, but in later stages, well-demarcated hyperdense masses with areas of calcification are observed . The presentation varies by stage; first, it is marked by a rapidly growing mass and swelling, which can raise reasonable concerns for a malignancy such as a soft tissue sarcoma. In later stages, the growth can be slowly progressive, and the lesion becomes firmer and localized, possibly leading to joint motion restriction . Our patient's clinical presentation and radiographic findings strongly suggested HO. However, due to the concerning characteristics of the mass, we performed an open biopsy to rule out malignancy. Although there is no consensus on the need for a biopsy, it ultimately confirms the diagnosis of a pseudotumor. Histopathological hallmarks include metal debris accumulation within macrophages and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrates . The histological description of pseudotumors has been included in aseptic lymphocyte-dominated vasculitis-associated lesions (ALVAL) . A classification system for ALVAL has been proposed by Campbell et al., focusing on three main histological characteristics: synovial lining integrity, inflammatory infiltrates, and tissue organization . Researchers have used this system to investigate the association between the extent of local histological reaction and postoperative functional outcomes of patients. Results suggest an inverse relationship between a high histological grade (i.e., ALVAL score > 9) and a corresponding decrease in functional knee metrics, such as the Oxford Knee Score . Nonetheless, despite our patient having a high ALVAL score and an Oxford Knee Score of 40, he remained asymptomatic at presentation, underscoring the diagnostic ambiguity of pseudotumors. Currently, there are no standardized guidelines for managing pseudotumors, and the treatment relies heavily on presentation and imaging findings . For asymptomatic patients, management focuses on serial radiographs to monitor for new implant-related complications such as component loosening . On the other hand, revision surgery is mainly reserved for symptomatic patients, particularly those with severe debilitating functional impairment, progressive imaging abnormalities, or findings suggestive of loosening . A consensus statement from the American Association of Hip and Knee Surgeons, the American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons, and Hip Society recommends avoiding reliance on a single diagnostic tool during decision-making to maintain an individualized approach with each patient . Therefore, we consider that the diagnostic workup and the treatment strategy should be addressed on a case-by-case basis. 4 Conclusion This report describes the emergence of a pseudotumor following TKA, initially diagnosed as HO. The definitive diagnosis was established through histopathological examination. Due to their vague presentation and non-specific imaging findings, a high clinical suspicion is crucial for early detection and management. Physicians should consider a comprehensive approach supported by a high index of suspicion to include pseudotumors within the differential diagnosis of knee periprosthetic masses. title: Simultaneous Post and Cone Fractures of a Polyethylene Insert in a Mobile-Bearing Posterior-Stabilized Total Knee Arthroplasty
case_text: A 72‐year‐old man who underwent a mobile‐bearing posterior‐stabilized total knee arthroplasty (PS‐TKA) 12 years earlier for osteoarthritis presented with recurrent right knee instability and pain on weight‐bearing. He denied any trauma. His medical history included atrial fibrillation and angina. He was independent in activities of daily living, ambulating with a walker. His body mass index was 36.7 kg/m2. On examination, the right knee had a range of motion from –15° of extension to 80° of flexion. There was no tenderness at rest, no heat, redness, or swelling, and no medial or lateral ligament dysfunction. Radiographs showed narrowing of the medial joint space suggestive of polyethylene (PE) insert wear. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated osteolysis and an intraosseous cyst on the lateral proximal tibia. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 4920 cells/μL and a C‐reactive protein level of 0.04 mg/dL. Radiographic criteria for aseptic loosening were not met, and osteolysis associated with increased PE wear particles was diagnosed. Revision of both femoral and tibial components was planned.
article_excerpt:
Introduction Aseptic loosening, due to the wear of polyethylene (PE) insert, is one of the failures after total knee arthroplasty (TKA) . Conversely, breakage of the PE insert itself is rare; nonetheless, awareness thereof is important, as it occurs rapidly and can severely affect knee function. Due to the post-cam mechanism of the PE insert, which is a distinctive feature of the posterior-stabilized (PS)-TKA, the postprocess of the PE insert suffers from mechanical stress by the femoral component during knee motion . Therefore, PS-TKAs, particularly those of the fixed-bearing design with stationary PE inserts, bear the risk of the post-fracture of the PE insert [ 3 , 4 ]. By contrast, the risk of post-fracture of the PE insert in mobile-bearing PS-TKAs may potentially be low because the free rotational motion of the PE insert reduces stress concentration [ 5 , 6 ]. The cone of the mobile-bearing PE insert, which is the center of the rotating motion, could be fractured after surgery, although this is rare [

,

,

]. Three previous studies on mobile-bearing PE inserts have reported on the exclusive occurrence of cone fractures. Furthermore, no reports exist regarding the simultaneous post and cone fractures of the PE insert. Thus, we reported a novel case of these simultaneous fractures of a PE insert in a mobile-bearing PS-TKA. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for the publication of this case report. Case history A 72-year-old male patient underwent TKA on the right knee due to osteoarthritis of the knee. The model used was a mobile-bearing PS-TKA with cross-linked PE (Vanguard RP, Zimmer Biomet, Warsaw, IN, USA) ( Fig. 1 ). He had retired from work and enjoyed walking as a hobby. Figure 1 Radiographs performed at the time of the primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA). (a) Preoperative radiograph of the right knee with osteoarthritis. (b) Postoperative anteroposterior view of the right knee radiograph. (c) Postoperative lateral view of the right knee radiograph. (d) Schema depicting mobile-bearing posterior stabilized TKA with a cone at the rotation center. (e) Schema depicting the high conformity of the articular surface. Seven years after the primary TKA, he consulted at our clinic due to right knee instability. There were no episodes of trauma; despite the presence of a subjective feeling of knee instability, there were no objective findings of knee instability on physical examination. No remarkable changes were observed between the postoperative images and current radiographs; thus, he underwent conservative treatment. The patient’s symptoms resolved immediately after the administration of conservative therapy, which comprised wearing a soft knee brace and performing rehabilitation therapy. Twelve years after the primary TKA, the patient consulted at our clinic again due to the recurrence of right knee instability. His medical history included the comorbidities of atrial fibrillation and angina pectoris, with no relevant family history, and he resided with his daughter. Initially, the patient was able to walk independently, using a walker. The patient was of Asian descent, with a height of 163 cm, a weight of 97.5 kg, and a body mass index (BMI) of 36.7 kg/m 2 . He presented with instability and pain in the right knee when weight-bearing and required assistance from others while walking. Tenderness and pain of the right knee at rest were not observed. The right knee range of motion was −15° of extension and 80° of flexion. No inflammation was present in the knee joint, as evidenced by the absence of heat, redness, and swelling. On physical examination, no medial or lateral ligament dysfunction was observed, and no gross or local inflammation was evident in the knee. Based on these findings, the knee instability was attributed to a failure of the prosthesis itself. Radiography showed joint space narrowing of the medial compartment, and wear of the PE insert was suspected ( Fig. 2 a and b). No progress was observed in the radiolucency between the prostheses and bone. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging revealed osteolysis and an intraosseous cyst on the lateral aspect of the proximal tibia ( Fig. 2 c and d). Biochemical laboratory results confirmed the absence of an inflammatory reaction, as evidenced by a white blood cell count of 4920 cells/μL and C-reactive protein of 0.04 mg/dL. Based on these findings, osteolysis of the proximal tibia associated with increased PE wear particles was diagnosed. Radiological findings did not meet the common definition of aseptic loosening because there was no appearance of a radiolucent line >2 mm or obvious migration of the components . Given the potential for direct contact between the femoral and tibial components, although it was not clear preoperatively, we planned for revision of both femoral and tibial components. Figure 2 Representative images before revision surgery. (a) Anteroposterior view of the radiograph showing joint space narrowing of the medial compartment, indicating the wear of the polyethylene insert. (b) Lateral view of the radiograph depicting contacted articular surface. (c) Osteolysis of the lateral side of proximal tibia is revealed on computed tomographic images (indicated by the yellow arrowheads). (d) Signal changes with low-signal intensity at T1-weighted (upper picture) and high-signal at T2-weighted (lower picture) magnetic resonance imaging are shown in the same area, indicating a cystic lesion (indicated by the yellow arrowheads). Revision, exchange of the femoral and tibial components, and PE insertion were performed under general anesthesia. The synovial membrane had proliferated, and the intra-articular soft tissues were stained black from the metallic debris ( Fig. 3 a). The femoral and tibial components were found to be loose, with bone loss on the lateral side of the proximal tibia ( Fig. 3 b and c). The post and cone of the PE insert had fractured simultaneously. The femoral and tibial components were in direct contact with each other, and the articular surface of the medial compartment was of a concave shape ( Fig. 4 ). A cemented fixed-bearing PS-TKA with a stem-type femoral/tibial component was used (Vanguard 360; Zimmer Biomet, Warsaw, IN, USA) ( Fig. 5 ). The PE insert was exchanged from the prerevision 10 mm to 14 mm at the time of the revision. Figure 3 Intraoperative images. (a) Intra-articular soft tissues stained black due to the metallic debris (indicated by the blue arrowheads) and the post-fracture of the polyethylene (PE) insert are observed (indicated by the yellow arrowheads). (b) The cone has been sheared off from the PE body, and the cone tip remains in the tibial tray after PE removal (indicated by the yellow arrowheads). (c) Bone loss on the lateral side of proximal tibia is shown (indicated by the yellow arrowheads). Figure 4 Removed components. (a) The femoral and tibial components are in direct contact with each other. The concave shape of the medial articular surface is revealed here (indicated by the yellow arrowheads). (b) Severe wear of the polyethylene (PE) insert of the medial compartment is shown (indicated by the yellow arrowheads). (c) Both the cone and post-fractures of the PE insert are depicted. Figure 5 Representative images after revision surgery. Revision surgery has been performed using a cemented fixed-bearing posterior-stabilized total knee arthroplasty with a stem, resulting in subsequent symptomatic and functional improvements of the knee. Anteroposterior and mediolateral instabilities were resolved post-revision. The patient was permitted to walk with immediate full weight-bearing after the revision surgery. One week postoperatively, he was able to walk independently, using a walker. He was discharged 3 weeks postoperatively, without pain. One year post-revision, physical examination revealed that he was able to walk independently, using a walker. His right knee range of motion was −5° of extension and −105° of flexion. Pain and instability of the right knee were absent. The Knee Society Scores-2011 for I (symptoms), II (satisfaction), III (expectancy), and IV (functional activity) were 23, 40, 9, and 49 points, respectively . The 12-item Forgotten Joint Score was 47.9 points . Discussion This novel case report describes the simultaneous post and cone fractures of a PE insert in a mobile-bearing PS-TKA. According to a systematic review, the incidence of a post-fracture in PS-TKA is less than 1% . The post-fracture of the PE insert is not a frequent complication of TKAs; nonetheless, the seriousness of this complication will be encountered by TKA surgeons who use PS-designed prostheses during their careers. The findings of a previous in vitro study demonstrated that the contact stress on the PE post increases rapidly, due to its high-conformity design, if the rotational movement of the mobile-bearing PE insert stops . In this case, the patient presented with instability 5 years prerevision. If the cone had been fractured at that time, the mobile-bearing rotational mechanism would have failed. Therefore, the contact stress had possibly increased rapidly in this prosthesis, finally resulting in the post-fracture. Furthermore, another in vitro study showed that PE wear particles are greater in PE designs with high-conformity articular surfaces . However, mobile-bearing TKA generally has favorable long-term outcomes, and aseptic loosening secondary to the wear of the PE insert is comparable to that of other designed prostheses . This may be a result of the mobile-bearing TKA design concept, which permits rotational movement, thus reducing the stress concentration . Therefore, in this case, the wear of the PE insert was speculated to have progressed severely because of the breakage of the rotational mechanism. The risk factors for the post-fracture of the PE insert remain controversial; however, men who are overweight and have high physical activity intensity levels are reported as at risk . In contrast, the risk factors for the cone fracture of PE inserts have not yet been detected statistically in a few cases. In 3 previous case reports regarding cone fractures of mobile-bearing PE inserts, all male patients were overweight, with an average BMI of 31.5 kg/m 2 [

,

,

]. In our case, the patient was overweight, with a BMI of 36.7 kg/m 2 , comparable to the patients in previous reports. As per these findings, the risks of post and cone fractures may be similar. Surgeons should consider potential PE breakage when selecting a TKA model for men who are overweight. Detection of PE breakage is important; nonetheless, the precise diagnosis of it based on symptoms may be challenging. Findings from a previous report showed that more than half of the patients with post-fractures of the PE insert did not present with pain . Thus, the risk of overlooking PE breakage exists if the attending doctor attempts to diagnose this condition based solely on pain. Conversely, instability has been found to occur in approximately 87% (61 of 70 cases) of the post-fracture PE inserts and is a major symptom . In the case of the cone fractures of the PE insert, the patient in the present case and patients in the 3 previous reports presented with instability. Therefore, the differential diagnosis inclusive of both post and cone fractures should be made by surgeons when treating patients with TKA who have suddenly presented knee instability, even in the absence of pain. We believe that surgeons had better be cognizant of this possibility, especially in increased-BMI male patients. This case demonstrated that a delayed diagnosis may lead to the severe wear of a PE insert. Summary We report a novel case of the simultaneous post and cone fractures of a mobile-bearing PS-TKA. The severe wear of the PE insert and direct contact between the femoral and tibial components were observed. Apart from the instability that occurred immediately prior to the consultations at our clinic, the patient was asymptomatic. A mobile-bearing, high-conformity PE insert can cause early severe wear if the rotational mechanism fails; however, a diagnosis based on pain alone may prove to be challenging. To diagnose a PE breakage, such as a post or cone fracture, the surgeon should be aware of the possibilities thereof, particularly in male patients who are overweight, presenting with instability. Future research endeavors should consider conducting large-scale cohort studies across diverse patient populations and settings, with a particular focus on refining diagnostic criteria and exploring potential risk factors beyond weight and sex associations. title: Brown tumor causing pathologic fracture of the ipsilateral femur and pelvis in a pregnant woman: a case report
case_text: A 30-year-old pregnant woman (gravida 2, abortus 1) at 32 weeks’ gestation presented with hypertension and left thigh pain, reporting one week of inability to bear weight. A Doppler ultrasound ruled out deep vein thrombosis. Radiographs of the left femur showed an aggressive lytic lesion in the distal femur with periosteal reaction. Laboratory studies revealed a serum calcium level of 4.13 mmol/L (reference range, 2.10–2.60 mmol/L). An open biopsy of the lesion demonstrated numerous multinucleated giant cells, but the radiographic appearance was inconsistent with a giant cell tumor.
article_excerpt: Introduction Brown tumors, or osteitis fibrosa cystica, are not true neoplasms but a manifestation of abnormal bone metabolism due to excessive osteoclastic activity in prolonged hyperparathyroidism . These lesions are commonly linked to primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism and may regress following treatment of the underlying condition . Persistent parathyroid hormone (PTH) elevation causes osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, leading to microfractures and hemorrhagic cystic spaces that progressively coalesce. The reddish-brown appearance of these lesions is due to hemosiderin deposition in the osteolytic cavities . Brown tumors may occur in multiple bones, often misdiagnosed as skeletal metastases [ 3 , 4 ]. They most commonly affect the craniofacial bones, long bones, pelvis, metacarpals, and ribs . Similar to metastatic bone disease, they can weaken bone structure and increase the risk of pathological fracture . Comprehensive diagnostics, including imaging, serum calcium, PTH, alkaline phosphatase, and bone scans, are crucial to assess for parathyroid adenomas. Pregnant patients require a tailored diagnostic approach to minimize fetal risk while managing hyperparathyroidism . Given their potential for misdiagnosis as malignant bone lesions and the risk of pathologic fractures, recognizing brown tumors is essential for orthopedic surgeons. Timely diagnosis and intervention are key for effective management. Case report A 30-year-old pregnant woman (G2A1) presented at 32 weeks’ gestation with hypertension and left thigh pain, unable to weight-bear for a week. Initial workup included an ultrasound to rule out deep vein thrombosis and radiographs, which showed an aggressive lesion in the distal femur with periosteal reaction ( Fig. 1A and B ). She was referred to orthopedic oncology, and a biopsy was arranged. Routine blood tests revealed markedly elevated serum calcium of 4.13 mmol/L (normal: 2.10–2.60 mmol/L). Histopathological analysis showed multinucleated giant cells, but radiographs were inconsistent with giant cell tumor (GCT), raising concern for a malignant lesion. Further investigation confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism, prompting consideration of a brown tumor. The patient was referred to head and neck surgery for parathyroidectomy evaluation. Figure 1 (A and B) Initial radiographs of the distal femur lesion. A multidisciplinary discussion involving orthopedic, maternal-fetal medicine, and head and neck teams determined the treatment plan. Further biopsy confirmed the brown tumor diagnosis, showing multinucleated giant cells, mononuclear stromal cells, bone resorption, and osteoclast clustering ( Fig. 2A–C ). Six days after the presentation, she was deemed suitable for parathyroidectomy. Although at high risk for pathologic fracture, she declined prophylactic fixation during pregnancy. Two days after a successful parathyroidectomy, she underwent an uncomplicated Cesarean section. As her calcium levels normalized, plans for femoral fixation were made post-childbirth. One week postpartum, the patient fell, resulting in a pathologic fracture of the left distal femur and ipsilateral iliac wing fracture ( Fig. 3A and B ). Figure 2 (A–C). Histopathologic images from biopsy specimen at 100× and 200× magnification, showing numerous multinucleated giant cells and mononuclear stromal cells with marked resorption of bone trabeculae and clustering of osteoclasts. Figures 3 (A and B) Pathologic fracture involving the left distal femur and left iliac bone. Definitive treatment of her distal femur fracture was performed the following day with a reamed, statically locked retrograde intramedullary nail after consultation with the orthopedic oncology team. The procedure was uncomplicated. For the iliac wing fracture, she was transferred to the local level I trauma center 5 days later for surgery by a pelvic and acetabular specialist. The fracture was addressed via a curvilinear approach to the iliac crest, followed by the application of a contoured pelvic reconstruction plate to the outer table of the iliac crest. Fixation was supplemented with an 8.0 mm partially threaded cannulated screw and advanced antegrade through the supraacetabular corridor ( Fig. 4 ). Figure 4 Intraoperative fluoroscopy from ORIF of the pelvis. At the time of pelvic fixation, a bone biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of a brown tumor. The patient underwent routine follow-up and was referred to endocrinology for ongoing calcium and vitamin D deficiency management. At over one year post-op, she had satisfactory clinical and radiographic healing with stable fixation ( Fig. 5A–C ). A skeletal survey identified additional resolving brown tumors in the right proximal humerus, left distal humerus, and bilateral tibia. By her last follow-up, all lesions had resolved, and she was discharged from orthopedic trauma and oncology care. Figure 5 (A–C) Final radiographs showing complete healing >1 year postoperatively. Discussion This case emphasizes the management of significant pathologic fractures secondary to a brown tumor in the setting of primary hyperparathyroidism, further complicated by pregnancy. Multidisciplinary collaboration was crucial to ensure comprehensive care. Aggressive bone lesions in young patients raise concern for serious conditions, with the differential diagnosis often including infection, hematologic malignancies, or primary bone sarcomas. Basic laboratory tests should always be part of the initial evaluation. In this case, elevated serum calcium pointed to a brown tumor, highlighting the role of laboratory markers in differentiating benign from malignant conditions. Brown tumors can mimic multiple skeletal metastases, but elevated calcium and PTH levels typically suggest primary hyperparathyroidism as the underlying cause [ 1 , 3 ]. They may also resemble multiple myeloma in cases of untreated, long-standing hyperparathyroidism . Diagnostic evaluation for bone lesions typically includes biopsy, though diagnostic uncertainty may persist. For instance, Zhong et al.  described a case where an aggressive bone lesion initially suggested malignancy, with a final diagnosis of brown tumor only after parathyroid hormone testing. Similarly, brown tumors share radiologic and histologic features with GCT . Primary hyperparathyroidism, the third most common endocrine disorder, should always be considered in the differential diagnosis [ 11 , 12 ]. A thorough history, physical exam, laboratory workup, and biopsy are key for definitive diagnosis. Although brown tumors are rare, surgical intervention is even less common as these lesions typically regress with the treatment of hyperparathyroidism . In most cases, parathyroidectomy alone resolves the lesions as overactive osteoclastic activity subsides. However, in this case, two significant pathologic fractures required internal fixation to prevent long-term deformity and disability. Reports of internal fixation for pathologic fractures from brown tumors are scarce [ 14 , 15 ], and none have been documented involving the pelvic ring. This case suggests that surgical intervention is warranted when fractures significantly impair patient independent function or ambulation. Otherwise, lesions can be monitored and typically resolve after treating the underlying hyperparathyroidism.

title: Proximal Femoral Erosion: A Sequelae of Psuedoaneursym Formation Following Operative Fixation of an Intertrochanteric Neck of Femur Fracture
case_text: A 72-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease fell while intoxicated and presented with left hip pain and decreased mobility. Radiographs revealed a left intertrochanteric femoral-neck fracture, and he underwent fixation with a dynamic hip screw without immediate complication. Postoperatively, he reported medial thigh pain; radiographs were interpreted as normal and he was discharged. Fifteen months later, he returned with persistent left thigh pain and progressive swelling. Examination showed a large, fixed mass in the left anteromedial thigh; distal pulses and sensation were intact. Pelvic radiographs demonstrated union of the fracture and a well-positioned screw but revealed scalloping of the medial femoral cortex and protrusion of screws beyond the cortex. Ultrasound was inconclusive. A magnetic resonance image, performed to exclude sarcoma, showed an asymmetric expansion of the left proximal thigh by an 11 × 11 × 12 cm heterogeneous lesion impinging on the neurovascular bundle. Differential diagnosis at this stage included vascular aneurysm formation, osteomyelitis with abscess formation, and a neoplastic process.
article_excerpt: Introduction Internal fixation of proximal femur fractures is one of the most common orthopedic procedures performed around the world. Vascular complications following these surgeries are rare with an incidence of 0.2%. 1 A recent review found the majority of vascular complications to be iatrogenic, and pseudoaneurysms accounted for 68% of vascular complications. 2 Nearly 94% of total vascular complications required procedural intervention; 56% needing an open procedure (mostly direct vessel repair or neck aneurysm ligation) and 35% managed with angiographic embolization. Almost 70% of total vascular injuries had an uneventful recovery following management. 2 As such, vascular complications need to be recognized and effectively managed to reduce morbidity. These vascular complications typically present with localized pain (68%) and swelling (92%) over the affected area; these signs are even more common with pseudoaneurysms. 2 This case report examines the development of a profunda femoris artery pseudoaneurysm following internal fixation of an intertrochanteric neck of femur fracture. To the authors’ knowledge, this is the first reported case of femoral scalloping present on a postoperative radiograph as a radiological sign of a profunda femoris artery pseudoaneurysm. Case Report In January 2014, a 72-year-old gentleman with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease attended an emergency department following a fall while intoxicated. He presented with left hip pain and decreased mobility. Radiographs demonstrated a left intertrochanteric neck of femur fracture. He underwent operative fixation with a dynamic hip screw (DHS) [ Figure 1 ]. There were no immediate complications; however, postoperatively, he reported pain in his medial thigh. Further radiographs were reported as unremarkable and the patient was discharged home without significant delay. Figure 1 Postoperative anteroposterior pelvis radiograph showing a left dynamic hip screw in situ In April 2015, due to a persistent pain and swelling in his left thigh, the patient represented to the emergency department and was referred to fracture clinic. Since his initial surgery, the thigh swelling had been gradually increasing in size and he frequently took dihydrocodeine to manage the pain. Further questioning revealed that the patient presented to the emergency department 2 weeks following surgery; however, a pelvic radiograph was reported as normal and he was discharged without followup. On examination, there was a large, fixed mass in the left anteromedial aspect of his thigh. Distal pulses were palpable and distal sensation was intact. A pelvic radiograph showed arthrosis of the left hip and union of the proximal femur fracture, with a DHS present in a satisfactory position. There was scalloping of the medial femoral cortex and extrusion of the screws past the medial femoral cortex [ Figure 2 ]. Ultrasound was inconclusive. A magnetic resonance image was performed to exclude sarcoma, which demonstrated an asymmetric expansion of the left proximal thigh and an 11 cm × 11 cm × 12 cm heterogeneous lesion that was likely to be impinging upon the neurovascular bundle. Differential diagnosis at this stage included vascular aneurysm formation, osteomyelitis with abscess formation, or a neoplastic process. Figure 2 Anteroposterior pelvis radiograph showing left dynamic hip screw in situ with medial scalloping of the femur, with screws penetrating beyond the medial cortex at 15-month followup A computed tomographic angiogram of the lower limb confirmed a large hematoma and pseudoaneurysm measuring 24.2 mm from a branch of the left profunda femoris artery. The patient underwent coil embolization of the pseudoaneurysm with an uneventful recovery [Figure 3a and b ]. At 3-month followup, the patient's symptoms had completely resolved. At 2½-year telephonic followup, the patient continues to report no further symptoms. Figure 3 Left proximal femur with left dynamic hip screw in situ and digital subtraction angiography of the left common femoral artery demonstrating a profunda branch aneurysm (a) and following coil embolization (b) Discussion Iatrogenic injury to the profunda femoris artery following operative fixation of intertrochanteric neck of femur fracture is rare and possibly underreported. 3 Several case reports show variations of a profunda femoris artery injury in both acute and chronic presentations. 4 5 6 Neuburer et al. found that vascular lesions affected the deep femoral artery significantly more than the superficial femoral artery. 2 Pseudoaneurysm formation was more frequent and there was significant diagnostic delay (36 days vs. 2 days) than identifying other vascular lesions. In this case report, injury is hypothesized to have occurred during initial overdrilling of the proximal femoral cortex from a lateral-to-medial direction prior to screw placement in the DHS plate. The patient's postoperative pain and swelling in the groin was caused by the pseudoaneurysm and, in this case, possibly a re-bleed within the pseudoaneurysm, prompting the patient to seek further medical attention. What is unique about this particular case is the scalloping of the medial femoral cortex caused by the mass effect of the expanding hematoma and subsequent remodeling of the medial femoral cortex. Although the screws are proud of the medial cortex, a decision was made not to remove the metalwork due to the risk of subsequent femoral fracture. A full workup was also performed to exclude other benign and malignant causes of femoral scalloping. Iatrogenic injury to the profunda femoris artery during operative fixation of proximal femur fractures is potentially a preventable occurrence. This is likely best achieved by avoiding overdrilling of the medial femoral cortex prior to positioning of shaft screw fixation in the DHS plate. This case report serves as a reminder to all surgeons on the potential dangers of overdrilling and the need to be mindful during this process. While uncommon, vascular complications do occur following operative fixation of proximal femur fractures. The key learning messages from this case report are to avoid overdrilling of the medial femoral cortex prior to shaft screw fixation in the DHS plate and to be mindful of vascular complications in any postoperative patient presenting with localized pain and swelling over the proximal thigh. Evidence of vascular complication should be looked for on both clinical examination and subsequent imaging in symptomatic patients. Evidence of remodeling cortical bone not keeping with postfracture healing may be a radiological sign of hematoma and profunda femoris artery pseudoaneurysm and should prompt further investigation and management to ensure satisfactory patient outcomes. title: Unusual Painful Muscle Spasm in a Dialysis-Dependent Patient with Progressive Cervical Kyphosis
case_text:
A 51-year-old man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis for over 10 years secondary to nephrotic syndrome initially presented with progressive numbness of the extremities, clumsy hands, and difficulty walking without assistance. Examination revealed spastic gait disturbance and increased muscle tone. His serum creatine kinase (CK) was slightly elevated at 315 U/l. Cervical laminoplasty was performed for cervical myelopathy attributed to destructive spondyloarthropathy, and his neurologic symptoms improved postoperatively.

Two months later, he developed intractable, cramp-like muscle pain throughout his body, occurring paroxysmally with severe spasticity. His pain was rated 10/10 on the numerical rating scale, with painDETECT and Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory scores of 28 and 79, respectively. Ketamine provided only partial relief, and conservative measures failed to control his symptoms.

Plain radiographs revealed progressive destructive changes at C4–C5 and C5–C6 and marked kyphosis of the subaxial spine with a C2–7 angle of –53°. Laboratory studies showed a markedly elevated CK of 999 U/l. Neurology and nephrology consultations were obtained, and the differential diagnosis included myopathy, electrolyte imbalance, and adverse drug reactions, but no clear cause was identified.
article_excerpt: 1. Introduction Patients with cervical myelopathy may present with a variety of manifestations, including increased tonus of the skeletal muscles. However, there are no previous reports of cervical compressive myelopathy in which the main manifestation is a painful muscle spasm. We herein report a case of cervical myelopathy due to destructive spondyloarthropathy (DSA) with a severe painful muscle spasm. 2. Case Report A 51-year-old man presented to our hospital due to symptoms of myelopathy. He had been undergoing hemodialysis due to chronic kidney failure associated with nephrotic syndrome for over 10 years. He complained of numbness in the extremities and clumsy hands, and he was unable to walk without assistance. Spastic gait disturbance associated with increased muscle tonus was observed, and his serum CK level remained slightly high (315 U/l). Cervical laminoplasty was performed for cervical myelopathy related to cervical DSA ( Figure 1 ). The postoperative course was uneventful. His numbness and clumsy hands improved, and he became ambulatory. Two months after the initial surgery, however, his condition started to deteriorate. He developed unusual intractable pain throughout his whole body, and cramp-like muscle pain was observed paroxysmally and frequently with severe spasticity. Regarding the pain intensity, the numerical rating scale (NRS) score (wherein 0 = no pain and 10 = the worst pain), painDETECT score , and neuropathic pain symptom inventory (NPSI)  were 10, 28, and 79, respectively. While his pain was partially relieved by the administration of ketamine, his symptoms were disabling and not sufficiently managed by conservative treatment. Plain radiographs showed the progression of destructive changes at the C4/5 and C5/6 levels. A marked progression of kyphosis of the subaxial spine was noted with a C2-7 angle of -53° ( Figure 2 ). A laboratory examination revealed that his serum level of CK was extremely high (999 U/l). With a marked elevation of CK, we first consulted neurologists and nephrologists regarding the possible underlying pathology. The differential diagnosis included myopathy, an electrolyte imbalance, and an adverse drug reaction; however, the cause of the patient's condition remained unclear. Therefore, we performed additional surgery to resolve the deteriorated destructive changes in the cervical spine, which we assumed to be potentially responsible for his symptoms. In the first stage of surgery, cervicothoracic posterior spinal fusion was performed from C2 to T2 using pedicle screws at the C2, C3, C7, T1, and T2 vertebral levels. In the second stage of surgery (10 days after the first stage), anterior spinal fusion was performed from C3 to C7 with an autologous iliac bone graft and a titanium plate ( Figure 3 ). The patient's intractable pain disappeared within 2 weeks after surgery. On comparing the pain intensity between before and after the two-stage surgery, the NRS score improved from 10 to 1, the painDETECT score changed from 28 to 10, and the NPSI score changed from 79 to 10. The serum level of CK was also normalized after the two-stage surgery ( Figure 4 ). At 10 months after surgery, he was able to walk without any support. The patient and his family were informed that data from the case would be submitted for publication and gave their informed consent. 3. Discussion Our patient had debilitating pain associated with a severe muscle spasm, an uncommon manifestation of cervical compressive myelopathy, which was triggered by subtle stimulation. Marked serum CK elevation (approximately 1,000 U/l) suggested muscle tissue damage caused by excessive muscle spasm. Of note, the patient's serum CK level was normalized once the painful muscle spasms were resolved after revision surgery. To our knowledge, there have been no reports regarding the association between cervical compressive myelopathy and the increase in serum CK due to spasticity. Colachis and Rea reported a case of T4 paraplegia with recurrent episodes of severe spasticity and CK elevation associated with intrathecal baclofen (ITB) withdrawal. The authors hypothesized that the elevated CK level, as a clear indication of severe hyperexcitability and contractibility of muscle fibers in muscle breakdown, was associated with a severe increase in spasticity due to ITB withdrawal . Similarly, in the present case, we assumed that the excessive muscle contraction associated with spasticity resulted in the dissolution of muscle and marked CK elevation. It is widely accepted that patients with cervical cord compression often present with neuropathic pain . The changes of painDETECT and NPSI scores indeed suggest that neuropathic pain played a role in the present case as well. However, severe damage to muscle tissue—as evidenced by the patient's CK elevation—indicated a distinct pathomechanism besides neuropathic pain in this case. Interestingly, a similar symptom known as painful tonic spasm has been reported in patients with various neurological disorders, including multiple sclerosis  and neuromyelitis optica . Further studies and the accumulation of more case reports are warranted to clarify the pathomechanism of a painful muscle spasm in cervical compressive myelopathy patients. Physicians should be alert to the possibility of pain caused by an excessive muscle spasm in cervical myelopathy patients, in particular for those with severe spasticity.

title: Subchondral Insufficiency Fracture of Femoral head: Uncommon cause of Hip pain in Elderly
case_text: A 54-year-old man presented with two months of gradually progressive left hip pain, worse with prolonged walking and stair climbing and relieved by rest. He had no history of trauma, alcohol use, steroid intake, systemic illness, or prior hip pathology. On examination, flexion and internal rotation of the left hip were restricted at end range by pain, and there was tenderness over the anterior joint line. Plain radiographs of the pelvis and hips were unremarkable. His Harris hip score was 48, with pain as the predominant limiting factor. Magnetic resonance imaging of the left hip revealed a subchondral, discontinuous, serpiginous radiolucent line parallel to the articular surface that was hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted images, with adjacent T2 hyperintensity due to marrow edema. Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry showed osteopenia (average T score –1.4), and serum vitamin D₃ was 8 ng/mL.
article_excerpt: Introduction Subchondral insufficiency fracture (SIF) is the fracture occurring in femoral head without any trauma and usually presents with hip pain [ 1 , 2 ]. The two categories of patients commonly affected are young military recruits and old patients with poor bone stock. It has also been reported in recipients of renal transplant, rheumatoid arthritis patients taking steroids and after liver transplant [ 3 , 4 ]. Osteonecrosis and transient osteoporosis are the main differential diagnosis. Few patients may respond to conservative treatment [ 5 , 6 ] But some may require surgical intervention due to rapid progression of disease [ 2 , 7 , 8 , 9 ]. Here we report this rare case in 54 year male who responded well to conservative treatment. Case Report Fifty four year old male came with pain in left hip since two months. Pain started insidiously and was gradually progressing, aggravated by prolonged walking, climbing stairs and relieved with rest. Patient was already under treatment with analgesics for complaints of occasional back pain. There was no history of alcoholism, trauma, steroid intake or any systemic illness or childhood hip pathology like Perthes disease or any septic hip disease. Clinical examination of hip showed terminal restriction of flexion and internal rotation due to pain. Tenderness was present on anterior joint line. No other positive finding could be elicited in affected or opposite hip. Radiograph of the affected hip with pelvis did not reveal any abnormality ( Fig. 1 ). Harris hip score was 48 with pain as most significant factor. MRI showed subchondral, discontinuous, serpiginous radiolucent line parallel to articular surface which was hypointense in both T1 and T2 images and with adjacent hyperintense shadow in T2 due to marrow edema. This picture was suggestive of subchondral insufficiency fracture ( Fig. 2 ). DEXA scan revealed low T scores at all sites average of -1.4 indicating osteopenia. Vitamin D3 levels were below normal (8ng/ml). Figure 1 Radiograph of pelvis with both hips showing no obvious abnormality Figure 2 MRI T1 image showing subchondral, discontinuous, serpiginous dark line parallel to articular surface with surrounding oedema Patient was kept non weight bearing and was given standard treatment for osteopenia including Vitamin D3 supplementation and alendronate. After six weeks, movements improved with minimal pain on exertion. Harris hip score improved to 80 and repeat MRI at three months showed decrease in bone edema and blurring of fracture line indicating healing. MRI at 6 months showed complete healing of the lesion ( Fig. 3 ). At one year follow up patient was completely asymptomatic and was independently able to carry out his activities of daily living. Figure 3 Six month follow up MRI showing healing of the lesion. Discussion The term subchondral insufficiency fracture of femoral head was coined by Bangil et al in 1996 . SIF occurs when physiological stress is applied to weakened bone due to poor mineralization or decreased elastic resistance. So it is most commonly seen in postmenopausal osteoporotic females  but can be seen in young military recruits as stress fractures [ 11 , 12 ]. In a histopathological study done on surgically resected 7718 femoral heads by Yamamoto et al incidence was highest above the age of 60 but it is also seen in third and fourth decade . SIF may be underdiagnosed due to difficulty in diagnosis. It needs to be differentiated from osteonecrosis and transient osteoporosis which may be difficult at times. Pain in hip in transient osteoporosis even though is similar to pain in osteonecrosis; pain in transient osteoporosis gradually progresses reaching highest intensity in 6-8 weeks and then gradually decreases over next 6-12 months. But pain in osteonecrosis is gradually progressive and worsening. Men above 40 who are alcoholic or taking steroids are the typical presentation for osteonecrosis. Transient osteoporosis of hip is self-limiting condition usually seen in middle aged males or in third trimester of pregnancy which is not the usual age group for SIF. Further studies needs to be done to find out correlation between these two. MRI shows bone marrow edema in all these three conditions. In osteonecrosis MRI shows hypointense band with concavity to articular surface, in SIF this band is serpiginous, with convexity to articular surface and usually discontinuous [ 13 , 14 ]. But few reports mention shape of hypointense band concave to articular surface in SIF . Contrast enhancement proximal to hypointense band in head may be additional MRI finding that can differentiate SIF from osteonecrosis and transient osteoporosis which is due to viable bone in SIF as opposed to dead bone in osteonecrosis . This low intensity band in SIF corresponds to subchondral fracture and repair tissue [ 2 , 12 ]. This area contains irregularly arranged fracture callus, reactive cartilage and granulation tissue. Subchondral collapse, gradual deterioration of bone marrow edema in MRI, disorganization and collapse of femoral head are the MRI features which differentiates osteonecrosis from SIF and transient osteoporosis. Transient osteoporosis of hip shows bone marrow edema and low signal intensity linear patterns in T1 in subchondral region extending to intertrochanteric region which will be high intensity in T2 . Bone trabaculae are thick in osteoarthritis but in SIF they are thin and sparse . Treatment of transient osteoporosis of hip is supportive; as various treatment modalities has failed to conclusively show any benefit in this condition. Protected weight bearing, NSAIDS and physiotherapy as soon as patient is comfortable are the usual components of treatment. Abductor strengthening exercises should be started at the earliest to prevent contractures. Aim of treatment is to prevent microfractures and pathological stress fractures. In those patients with no collapse on MRI heal with conservative treatment of osteoporosis, protected weight bearing and restriction of activities. Those having collapse require arthroplasty . Prognosis of SIF is still unclear and may depend on extent of fracture, severity of osteoporosis (Singh’s index), weight, activity level of the patient and age . Miyanishi et al studied 27 patients having SIF of femoral head to identify the risk factors for THA. Patient age was the only statistically significant risk factor with elderly patients having more chances of undergoing THA . As per Iwasaki et al who studied MRI of 25 patients having SIF of femoral head, band length and band length ratio may be predictive of collapse of head in cases of SIF. Band length being measured at the slice having maximum length of band in T1 wt coronal images of hip. Band length ratio represents length of fracture line relative to length of weight bearing portion at femoral head slice . Conclusion In short subchondral insufficiency fracture of femoral head is common in elderly osteoporotic patients, uncommon in healthy young adults. It needs to be diagnosed at the earliest by excluding osteonecrosis and transient osteoporosis. MRI will help in diagnosing it early and may help to determine prognosis. Patients without collapse has good prognosis as these are likely to respond to conservative treatment, but others may require arthroplasty so follow up is necessary once subchondral insufficiency fracture of femoral head is diagnosed. Clinical Message Elderly patients presenting with persistent hip pain without any abnormality on plain radiograph should be suspected for Subchondral insufficiency fractures. MRI is essential for diagnosis and early diagnosis can avoid progression of disease and need for surgical
